subject: EM
title: Water, oceans & fisheries
sub: Water supply, pollution, disease, oceans, fisheries
strategyIntro: Environmental Management has no Core or Extended split. The full exam is Paper 1 (theory: short questions, then longer questions using source material) and Paper 2 (management in context, based on one country). Most marks come from reading sources and building arguments.

strategy.title: Quote the data
points: Most marks come from graphs, tables and maps.
Use figures with units: “fell from 62% to 41%” scores; “it fell” doesn’t.
Describe the overall trend first, then give the highest, lowest or any exception.

strategy.title: The 6-mark argument
points: Usually one per paper: discuss a statement for and against.
Structure: two points for, two against, then a conclusion.
Each point needs a reason: say why it matters, not just what it is.

strategy.title: Use named examples
points: Name a real dam, river or fishery where you can (e.g. the Peruvian anchovy fishery, North Sea cod).
On Paper 2, link every answer back to the country in the source. General answers score lower.

strategy.title: Fieldwork comes up every year
points: Know sampling, quadrats, questionnaires and how to make them reliable.
Evaluate a method: one strength, one weakness, one improvement.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
Weigh up both sides and finish with a judgement.
quizIntro: These are not exam-format questions (EM has no multiple choice). Use them to check the facts are secure before you try the longer questions.
flashIntro: Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: About 97% of Earth’s water is salt water. Of the fresh water, most is frozen in ice caps and glaciers; under 1% of all water is easy to reach.
Liquid water turning into water vapour, using heat from the Sun, e.g. from oceans, lakes and soil.
Loss of water vapour from plant leaves through the stomata.
Water vapour cooling and turning back into liquid droplets, forming clouds.
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Infiltration: water soaking into the soil. Surface runoff: water flowing over the ground into rivers.
A layer of porous rock that stores groundwater, which can be pumped up through wells.
Water that is safe to drink.
Removing salt from sea water to make fresh water (e.g. reverse osmosis). Reliable but expensive and uses a lot of energy.
A dam and reservoir built for several uses: HEP, irrigation, water supply, flood control and recreation.
Point source: pollution from one place, e.g. a factory pipe. Non-point (diffuse): from a wide area, e.g. runoff from many farms.
Contains organic matter (decomposed by bacteria, using up oxygen) and pathogens that spread disease.
Fertilisers (cause eutrophication), pesticides and animal waste washed into rivers.
Toxic chemicals and heavy metals such as mercury and lead released into water. They can bioaccumulate in food chains.
Warm water released from power stations or factories. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen.
Oil coats birds’ feathers (they lose waterproofing and insulation), blocks light and is toxic to marine life.
Not biodegradable. Animals become entangled or eat it; microplastics enter food chains.
Organisms whose presence or absence shows how polluted water is, e.g. stonefly nymphs = clean; bloodworms, sludge worms = polluted.
Biochemical oxygen demand: oxygen used by microorganisms breaking down organic matter. High BOD = heavy organic pollution.
Screening, settling (sludge removed), bacteria breaking down organic matter with air bubbled through, settling again, then release; sludge can make biogas.
A microorganism that causes disease, e.g. a bacterium, virus or protoctist.
A disease caught by drinking or using water containing pathogens, e.g. cholera, typhoid.
Caused by a bacterium spread in water contaminated with faeces. Causes severe diarrhoea and dehydration, which can kill within hours.
Treating dehydration (e.g. from cholera) with clean water containing salts and sugar.
Safe drinking water (treated, boiled), sanitation (toilets, sewers), handwashing, vaccination.
Safe disposal of human waste, e.g. toilets and sewers, so it does not contaminate water.
Making water potable: filtration (e.g. through sand) removes particles; chlorination kills pathogens.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, e.g. the mosquito for malaria.
Caused by a Plasmodium parasite, passed on when a female Anopheles mosquito bites. Mosquitoes breed in still water.
Insecticide-treated bed nets, draining standing water, spraying insecticide, fish that eat larvae, antimalarial drugs.
Food (fish, shellfish, seaweed), minerals (oil, gas, sand, gravel, salt), energy (tidal, wave, offshore wind), transport, tourism.
Shallow sea (under about 200 m deep) around continents. Light reaches far down, so plankton thrive: most fishing happens here.
Microscopic algae that photosynthesise near the surface. The producers at the base of most marine food chains.
Cold, nutrient-rich water rising from the deep ocean to the surface. Plankton grow fast, making rich fishing grounds, e.g. off Peru.
Large movements of surface water driven by winds. Warm and cold currents move heat around the planet.
Trade winds weaken; warm water spreads east across the Pacific to South America and stops upwelling off Peru. Fish catches collapse.
Heavy rain and floods in Peru and Ecuador; drought in Australia and Indonesia.
Sea up to 200 nautical miles from a country’s coast, where it controls fishing and mineral rights.
Very high biodiversity; protect coasts and support fisheries and tourism. Threatened by warming (bleaching), pollution and destructive fishing.
Catching fish faster than they can reproduce, so the stock (population) falls.
The largest catch that can be taken from a fish stock every year without the stock falling.
Unwanted species caught by accident, e.g. dolphins, turtles, young fish. Often thrown back dead.
Dragging a large net through the water or along the seabed. Bottom trawling damages seabed habitats.
A net that encircles a shoal and is then pulled closed at the bottom like a drawstring purse.
A very long line with thousands of baited hooks. Bycatch includes seabirds, sharks and turtles.
A limit on the amount of a species that may be caught in a period.
A minimum size for the holes in nets, so young fish can escape and grow to breed.
An area of sea where fishing is restricted or banned (no-take zone), so stocks can recover.
Raising fish or shellfish in enclosures. Can cause waste pollution, disease spreading to wild fish, escapes, and mangrove clearance.

quiz.q: Most of Earth’s fresh water is stored in:
quiz.why: Roughly two thirds of fresh water is frozen; most of the rest is groundwater.

quiz.q: Which process forms clouds?
quiz.why: Rising air cools, so water vapour condenses into tiny droplets.

quiz.q: Globally, which sector uses the most fresh water?
quiz.why: About 70% of fresh water taken worldwide goes to farming.

quiz.q: A disadvantage of desalination is that it:
options: Uses a lot of energy and is expensive
quiz.why: It also produces very salty brine that must be disposed of.

quiz.q: Wells obtain water from:
quiz.why: A well is dug or drilled down below the water table into a water-bearing rock layer.

quiz.q: “Economic water scarcity” means:
options: There is enough water, but people cannot afford the infrastructure to reach it
Water is too expensive to export
All water is used by industry
quiz.why: Physical scarcity is when there is not enough water at all; economic scarcity is lack of money for pipes, wells and treatment.

quiz.q: Which organism in a river shows clean, well-oxygenated water?
quiz.why: Stonefly nymphs need high oxygen levels. The other three can survive in low-oxygen, polluted water.

quiz.q: Thermal pollution harms fish because:
options: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen
quiz.why: Fish also respire faster in warm water, so they need more oxygen just as less is available.

quiz.q: A high BOD in a river shows that:
options: There is a lot of organic matter being decomposed
quiz.why: Decomposers break down the organic matter (e.g. sewage) and use up oxygen as they do.

quiz.q: Which is a non-point (diffuse) source of pollution?
options: A pipe from a paper mill
quiz.why: It enters the river along a long stretch rather than at one point, so it is hard to control.

quiz.q: Oil spills kill seabirds mainly because the oil:
options: Coats their feathers, so they lose waterproofing and insulation
Kills all their prey at once
quiz.why: Oiled birds get cold, cannot fly or float, and swallow oil while preening.

quiz.q: Malaria is passed to humans by:
options: The bite of an infected female mosquito
quiz.why: Malaria is water-related (mosquitoes breed in water) but not waterborne.

quiz.q: Draining areas of standing water helps control malaria because it:
options: Removes places where mosquito larvae develop
quiz.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and the larvae live there.

quiz.q: Cholera kills mainly by causing:
quiz.why: That is why oral rehydration therapy saves so many lives.

quiz.q: Chlorine is added to drinking water to:
quiz.why: Filtration removes particles; chlorination kills bacteria such as the one that causes cholera.

quiz.q: Why do cholera outbreaks often follow floods?
options: Sewage mixes with drinking water and pipes are damaged
quiz.why: Crowded camps with no sanitation add to the risk.

quiz.q: Most fishing grounds are on continental shelves because:
options: The water is deep and cold
Shallow water lets light reach plankton, and rivers bring nutrients
quiz.why: More plankton means more food for fish.

quiz.q: Upwelling brings to the surface:
quiz.why: The nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) feed phytoplankton when they reach sunlit water.

quiz.q: During an El Niño year off Peru:
options: Warm water stops upwelling, and anchovy catches fall
quiz.why: Less nutrient-rich water means less plankton, so anchovies die or move away.

quiz.q: A country’s Exclusive Economic Zone extends:
quiz.why: Within its EEZ a country controls fishing and seabed resources such as oil and gas.

quiz.q: Which is a non-living resource from the oceans?
quiz.why: Other non-living resources: sand and gravel, salt, manganese nodules.

quiz.q: A larger minimum mesh size helps to conserve fish stocks because:
options: Young fish can escape and grow to breed
quiz.why: Fish must breed at least once before being caught if the stock is to replace itself.

quiz.q: Which fishing method does most damage to seabed habitats?
quiz.why: Heavy nets dragged along the seabed destroy corals, sponges and breeding areas.

quiz.q: Sonar and GPS on fishing boats increase the risk of overfishing because they:
options: Help boats find and catch whole shoals
quiz.why: Technology raised catches far above what stocks could replace.

quiz.q: Which is a problem caused by fish farming?
options: Waste and disease spreading to wild fish
It damages the seabed by trawling
quiz.why: Farmed salmon, for example, can spread sea lice to wild fish; feed is often made from wild-caught fish.

quiz.q: Fishing quotas can fail because:
options: They are hard to enforce, and fish may be caught illegally or discarded
They only apply to farmed fish
quiz.why: Fishers may land extra fish illegally, or throw back dead fish that would take them over quota.

examIntro: Paper 1 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme. The data questions give a small table in the question: quote the figures in your answer.

exam.q: State two ways water can be supplied to a town.
points: Wells / boreholes into aquifers
Rivers
Reservoirs behind dams
Desalination of sea water
Rainwater harvesting
Water transfer by pipeline or canal

exam.q: Water use by sector (%). Country P (high-income): agriculture 30, industry 50, domestic 20. Country Q (low-income): agriculture 85, industry 5, domestic 10. Compare the water use of the two countries and suggest reasons for the differences.
points: Q uses a much higher share for agriculture (85% compared with 30%)
P uses a much higher share for industry (50% compared with 5%)
P uses a higher share for domestic use (20% compared with 10%)
Q’s economy depends more on farming / needs irrigation in a dry climate
P is more industrialised
P’s homes have piped water and appliances such as washing machines and showers
exam.note: Any 4; at least one must quote figures for both countries.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of multipurpose dam schemes to manage water.
points: Benefit: HEP, a renewable source of electricity
Benefit: reliable water supply for irrigation, homes and industry all year
Benefit: flood control downstream
Benefit: recreation, tourism and fishing on the reservoir
Cost: land flooded, so people are relocated and habitats lost
Cost: sediment trapped behind the dam, so the reservoir silts up and farmland downstream gets less fertile silt
Cost: very expensive; blocks fish migration; disputes with countries downstream
Judgement: e.g. worthwhile if the people moved are compensated and an EIA is carried out
exam.note: Benefits and costs needed, plus a judgement. Max 5 without a judgement.

exam.q: State two sources of water pollution.
points: Untreated sewage
Fertiliser or pesticide runoff from farms
Industrial waste / heavy metals
Oil spills
Warm water from power stations
Plastic waste
Leachate from landfill / mining waste

exam.q: Describe how sewage is treated before the water is released into a river.
points: Screening removes large objects / grit
Primary settling tanks: solids sink as sludge
Aeration: air is bubbled through / trickling filter
Bacteria break down organic matter
Second settling tank removes bacteria and remaining solids
Water may be disinfected (e.g. UV) before release; sludge digested to make biogas or fertiliser

exam.q: Dissolved oxygen (mg per litre) at sites along a river: Site 1 (500 m above a sewage outlet) 9.5; Site 2 (at the outlet) 3.0; Site 3 (1 km below) 5.5; Site 4 (5 km below) 8.5. (a) Describe the pattern. (b) Explain the low value at Site 2. (c) Suggest why the oxygen level recovers downstream.
points: (a) High above the outlet (9.5) and falls sharply to 3.0 at the outlet
(a) Rises again downstream to 8.5 at 5 km, nearly back to the upstream level
(b) Sewage adds organic matter; bacteria decompose it
(b) Bacteria use up oxygen in respiration
(c) The organic matter has been broken down / diluted downstream
(c) Oxygen dissolves from the air (e.g. at riffles) / is released by water plants in photosynthesis

exam.q: Explain why cholera spreads more easily where there is no sanitation.
points: The faeces of infected people contain the cholera bacteria
Without toilets or sewers, faeces get into rivers, wells or water supplies
People drink or wash food in this untreated water
So more people are infected and the cycle continues

exam.q: Describe two methods of controlling malaria and explain how each works.
points: Bed nets treated with insecticide
Stop mosquitoes biting people at night / kill mosquitoes that land
Draining standing water / adding oil to ponds / fish that eat larvae
Removes or kills mosquito larvae, so fewer adult mosquitoes
Spraying insecticide indoors / antimalarial drugs
Kills adult mosquitoes / kills the parasite in the body

exam.q: Malaria cases in District Z (thousands): 2010 – 48; 2013 – 41; 2016 – 22; 2019 – 15; 2022 – 19. Bed nets were handed out from 2014. (a) Describe the trend. (b) Calculate the percentage decrease from 2010 to 2019. (c) Suggest two reasons why cases rose after 2019.
points: (a) Cases fell from 48 000 to 15 000 by 2019, then rose to 19 000
(a) Fastest fall 2013–2016 (41 000 to 22 000), after nets were handed out
(c) Nets wear out or are not replaced
(c) Mosquitoes resistant to insecticide / parasite resistant to drugs
(c) Heavy rain or floods made more breeding sites / funding for control cut

exam.q: State three resources, other than food, that people obtain from the oceans.
points: Oil and natural gas
Sand and gravel
Salt / minerals such as manganese nodules
Energy: tidal, wave or offshore wind
Fresh water by desalination
Transport routes / tourism

exam.q: Explain why areas of upwelling are rich fishing grounds.
points: Cold water rises from the deep ocean
It carries nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) to the surface
In sunlight, phytoplankton grow rapidly
Zooplankton and fish feed on them, so there are large fish populations

exam.q: Anchovy catch off a South American coast (million tonnes, made-up figures): 1970 – 12.0; 1973 – 1.8; 1980 – 0.8; 1994 – 9.5; 1998 – 1.5; 2004 – 10.5. El Niño events happened in 1972–73, 1982–83 and 1997–98. (a) Describe the changes in the catch. (b) Explain how El Niño causes the catch to fall. (c) Suggest one other reason why the catch stayed low in 1980.
points: (a) The catch varies greatly / falls and recovers
(a) Fell from 12.0 in 1970 to 1.8 in 1973; recovered to 9.5–10.5 by 1994 and 2004
(a) Sharp falls in El Niño years (1973 and 1998)
(b) Trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east over the cold water
(b) Upwelling stops, so no nutrients reach the surface
(b) Less plankton, so anchovies starve or move away
(c) Overfishing: too few adult fish were left to breed after the collapse
exam.note: Any 6, with at least one mark from each part.

exam.q: State what is meant by bycatch and give one example.
points: Species caught unintentionally / not the target species
Example: dolphins, turtles, seabirds, sharks or young fish

exam.q: Cod caught in Sea Area N (thousand tonnes): 1970 – 300; 1980 – 250; 1990 – 120; 2000 – 60; 2010 – 40. Number of large trawlers: 1970 – 80; 1980 – 110; 1990 – 140; 2000 – 120; 2010 – 70. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in the catch from 1970 to 2010. (b) Suggest why the catch fell between 1980 and 1990 even though the number of trawlers increased.
points: (b) More fishing effort but fewer fish: catch fell from 250 to 120 while trawlers rose from 110 to 140
(b) The stock was overfished: fish caught faster than they could reproduce / young fish caught before breeding

exam.q: Evaluate methods used to manage fish stocks.
points: Quotas limit the catch, but are hard to enforce
Larger mesh sizes let young fish escape, but bycatch of other species can continue
Closed seasons protect fish while they breed
Marine protected areas let stocks recover and fish spill over to nearby areas, but are hard to police
Bans on methods such as bottom trawling or drift nets protect habitats and reduce bycatch
Fish farming reduces pressure on wild stocks, but causes pollution and disease
Judgement: e.g. a combination works best, with monitoring and international agreement because fish cross borders
exam.note: At least two methods weighed up, plus a judgement. Max 5 without a judgement.
